name: paper
_comment: Stage A2: the reference's own workload shape, so 'does Bf-Tree transfer'
is asked the way the paper asked it.
Matched to benchmark/bench_bftree.toml ('storage' / 'read_only'):
100M records, key_len 16, VALUE = THE KEY (bench_bftree.rs does
`tree.insert(key, key)`, so a record is ~32 B, not our usual 116 B),
zipf 0.9, read=100, memory 1 GiB against ~3.2 GB of data (~30%).
Deliberately NOT matched, with reasons:
- storage backends StdDirect / IoUringPolling / IoUringBlocking.  SQLite's
unix VFS has no O_DIRECT and the comparison here is against
gold-standard SQLite, so porting one would change what we compare to.
It stays the honest prerequisite for the paper's ABSOLUTE numbers.
- 30 threads.  Blocked on A3 (--threads in bfbench.c).  Until that lands
this config understates the value of a cache hit: with many readers in
flight a hit removes queueing, not just one request.
TWO ARMS ON PURPOSE, and both get reported:
paper_raw       dist=zipf-raw, the rank used directly as the key, as the
reference does.  Hot keys are contiguous.
paper_scrambled dist=zipf, YCSB's FNV scramble, our long-standing
default.  Hot keys are scattered.
Neither is 'the honest one'.  Scrambling is the conservative choice and is
what YCSB does; raw is what the paper measured.  Quoting only the
flattering arm is the failure mode this config exists to prevent.
MEASURED (2026-09-16), controlled: same 4M-row dataset, same 16 MiB ring,
same promotion=30, 1.5M ops, only --dist varying:
dist       recs/page  B/record  cached  rec hit%   ops/s
So clustering is worth ~1.6x in mini-page occupancy and ~12% in bytes per
cached record -- real, but an order of magnitude less than a first guess
off an uncontrolled 20k-row spot check suggested (that comparison was
coverage, not distribution: 20k rows under a 1 MiB ring caches a large
fraction of the table, so even scrambled keys cluster, and BOTH dists gave
~11-13 recs/page there).  Measure occupancy at the coverage ratio you
actually intend to run; it is a property of the regime, not of the dist.
Note the direction of the hit rate: zipf-raw caches MORE records, hits on
FEWER of them, and is FASTER.  With contiguous hot keys the page cache
serves the hot set well on its own, so a record-cache miss is cheap and the
record hit rate stops being the metric that tracks throughput.  That is
worth knowing before B3 (full-page cache) is judged on hit rate.
Watch B/record and recs/page (report.py) as closely as the hit rate.  And
note evictions: at a 1 GiB ring these may well be 0, in which case the
warmup, not the capacity, is what the number is measuring.

experiments.name: paper_raw
_why: The replication target: reference workload, reference distribution.
If the mechanism transfers at all, it transfers here.

experiments.name: paper_scrambled
_why: Same everything, YCSB-scrambled keys.  The delta between the two arms
IS the measurement of how much of the paper's win depends on hot keys
being physically clustered -- which is also the precondition for the
full-page cache (B3) being an admission win rather than ring waste.
